abstract: The Workforce Almanac is a public-use directory of short-term workforce training providers in the United States, built by Harvard Kennedy School's Project on Workforce by combining four federal administrative data sources into a single deduplicated national file. Version 2.0, released August 2025, catalogs 20,211 providers, up from roughly 17,000 in the November 2023 launch. It defines its scope as post-high-school training lasting less than two years in which learners gain work-relevant skills, and it sorts providers into four types mapped onto a common taxonomy of 14 subtypes: sub-baccalaureate and non-degree-granting institutions of higher education (3,648, 18%), job training nonprofits (7,408, 37%), WIOA-eligible training providers on state Eligible Training Provider lists (29%), and federally Registered Apprenticeship sponsors (3,347, 16%). Coverage is all US states and territories, with regional and state-level breakdowns. This is infrastructure rather than research: it makes no claim about AI, employment, wages, or training outcomes, and reports no effect sizes. Its value to this project is as a denominator for reskilling capacity — how much training infrastructure exists, of what type, and where — against which displacement and exposure estimates elsewhere in the corpus can be set. Funded by Strada Education Foundation and the WorkRise Network; data and code published openly.
keyFindings: Version 2.0 (August 2025) catalogs 20,211 short-term workforce training providers nationally, up from roughly 17,000 in the November 2023 v1.0 launch.

Providers resolve into four types under a taxonomy of 14 subtypes: job training nonprofits (7,408, 37%), WIOA-eligible providers on state Eligible Training Provider lists (29%), sub-baccalaureate higher education institutions (3,648, 18%), and Registered Apprenticeship sponsors (3,347, 16%).
Scope is defined as post-high-school training lasting less than two years in which learners gain work-relevant skills — explicitly excluding four-year degree pathways.

Employer identification numbers were matched for 12,189 of 20,211 providers (60%); revenue and expense data exist for only about 20% (3,167 nonprofits via IRS, 1,406 higher education institutions via IPEDS).
The authors state the Almanac still underestimates the true number of US workforce training providers, so all counts should be read as a floor.
Contains no AI-related, employment-outcome, wage, or training-effectiveness measures — it is a directory of supply-side capacity, not an outcomes study.
methodology: Combines four publicly available administrative sources into one deduplicated provider file: IPEDS (Survey Year 2022) for public, nonprofit and for-profit postsecondary institutions primarily conferring sub-baccalaureate credentials; TrainingProviderResults.gov for WIOA-eligible providers on state Eligible Training Provider lists (period July 1 2019 to June 30 2023); IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File and Form 990 series (2022-2024) for job training nonprofits; and RAPIDS (FY2024 Q2) for federally Registered Apprenticeship sponsors. Nonprofit identification uses natural-language classification over organizational descriptions rather than NTEE codes alone, which is what drove most of the growth from v1.0 — many workforce providers had been filed under codes such as 'Children & Youth Services' or 'Rural Economic Development' and were missed. Records are enriched with EINs and, where available, IRS/IPEDS financial data. Authors: Joseph Fuller, Alexis Gable, Tessa Forshaw, Jacob Hale, Nathalie Gazzaneo, Gani Simsek.
qualifiers: The authors state plainly that the Almanac 'continues to underestimate the number of workforce training providers in the U.S.' Specific known gaps: for-profit two-year institutions operating without Title IV funding may not report to IPEDS and are therefore missing; institutions conferring majority four-year degrees are excluded even where they offer sub-baccalaureate credentials; the NLP classification of nonprofits produces false positives where an organization mentions training keywords without actually delivering training, though sampled false-positive rates were comparable to NTEE-based identification; and EIN and financial coverage is sparse, particularly for RAPIDS and TPR records. The four constituent sources have different vintages (IPEDS 2022, TPR 2019-2023, IRS 2022-2024, RAPIDS FY2024 Q2), so the file is not a clean point-in-time snapshot. Per-type counts published in the launch summary do not fully reconcile against the stated total, so type-level percentages are more reliable than raw type counts. Not peer-reviewed; a dataset release with accompanying methodology documentation.
